751.quote_or_event: “The value of penance has become visible, birth appears of no value! Look at the holy Harikêśa, the son of a Śvapâka, whose power is so great.”
751.explanation: After the outcaste-born monk Harikesa is first despised and then revered, the onlookers conclude that worth comes from austerity and virtue, not from birth or outward standing.
751.tie_back: The Kural says only wealth can turn people of no account into people of account; the Jain story makes the opposite claim, that it is penance that raised a man counted as nothing into one honoured by all.
751.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.37 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
751._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics normalised); it shares the Kural's theme of what makes a person count but credits penance rather than wealth, so it is a contrasting next-best match.

752.quote_or_event: “When (the priests) saw him coming up, emaciated by austerities, in a miserable condition, and with the poorest outfit, they laughed at him, the ruffians.”
752.explanation: The Brahmin priests at a sacrifice mock and then try to drive off the monk Harikesa because he looks destitute, until his spiritual power is revealed and they beg his forgiveness.
752.tie_back: The episode dramatises exactly what the Kural observes, that everyone scorns the person who appears to have nothing, though the Jain text condemns that scorn rather than treating it as a reason to get rich.
752.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
752._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the contempt shown to the poor-looking man matches the Kural's first line closely, while the other half (honour paid to the rich) is only implied by the story's reversal.

753.quote_or_event: “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
753.explanation: Mahavira's sermon pairs wealth with the image of a lamp in the dark, but warns that wealth gives no lasting protection and that the careless lose their way as when a lamp goes out.
753.tie_back: The Kural calls wealth an unfailing lamp that dispels darkness wherever its owner goes; the Jain verse uses the same lamp-and-darkness image to deny that wealth can be relied on, a pointed counter-reading.
753.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
753._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the shared lamp-in-darkness imagery linked to wealth is striking, but the Jain verse reaches the opposite verdict on wealth's reliability.

754.explanation: Hemacandra places honestly earned wealth first among the thirty-five qualities of the ideal Jain householder, so lawful earning is the foundation of lay virtue.
754.tie_back: The Kural says wealth gained by right means and without wrongdoing gives rise to virtue and happiness, and the Jain householder code makes exactly such honestly earned wealth the first mark of a good layman.
754.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, no. 1, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)
754._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com; a near one-to-one match on righteously earned wealth, though the list item itself does not state that such wealth produces virtue and happiness.

755.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
755.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that wealth gained by wrongful acts will be lost and leaves its owner bound by passion and hatred, binding further karma.
755.tie_back: The Kural tells us to let go of wealth that comes without compassion and love, and the Jain verse gives the reason: wealth gained by evil deeds does not stay and drags its owner into bondage.
755.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
755._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong thematic fit on rejecting ill-gotten wealth, though the Jain verse frames the wrong as evil deeds generally rather than naming compassion and love.

756.quote_or_event: “Multiply your gold and silver, your jewels and pearls, your copper, fine robes, and carriages, and your treasury; then you will be a true Kshattriya.”
756.explanation: Indra, testing the renouncing King Nami, tells him that filling the royal treasury is what makes a true king; Nami replies that mountains of gold would not satisfy greed and turns to austerity.
756.tie_back: The Kural lists the lawful sources of a king's treasury; the Jain text acknowledges the royal ideal of a full treasury but places it in the tempter's mouth, setting the king's wealth against the renouncer's freedom.
756.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.46 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
756._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it addresses the royal treasury but names no revenue sources (escheat, tolls, tribute), and the Jain text rejects the ideal, so this is a next-best match.

757.quote_or_event: “Yathavat atithau sadhau dine cha pratipatti-krt : Diligent in succoring the ascetics, the righteous and the needy.” … “Sadaya : Compassionate.”
757.explanation: Hemacandra's ideal householder, who first earns wealth honestly, is to be compassionate and to use his means in supporting ascetics, good people and the poor.
757.tie_back: The Kural pictures compassion as a child born of love and nursed by wealth, and the Jain layman's code likewise expects the compassionate householder to sustain the needy and the holy from his resources.
757.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, nos. 19 and 31, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)
757._accuracy_note: Both items verified verbatim on jainworld.com; together they link compassion with material support, but the list does not draw the Kural's parent-and-nurse relation between love, compassion and wealth.

758.quote_or_event: “Vyayam ayochitam kurvan : Spending in proportion to one's income.” … “Balabalam janan : Aware of one's own strength and weakness.”
758.explanation: Among the Jain householder's practical virtues are measuring expenditure against income and knowing one's own strength and weakness before acting.
758.tie_back: The Kural's man who starts a venture with money already in hand, watching safely as from a hilltop, reflects the same prudence the Jain householder code asks for in matching outlay to means and knowing one's capacity.
758.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, nos. 12 and 23, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)
758._accuracy_note: Both items verified verbatim on jainworld.com; they share only the general theme of financial prudence, with nothing on the Kural's specific point or its elephant-fight simile, so this is a next-best match.

759.quote_or_event: “Fight with your Self; why fight with external foes? He who conquers himself through himself, will obtain happiness.”
759.explanation: Nami tells Indra, who urges him to subdue rival kings, that the real battle is against one's own passions, and in the next verse he names them: the senses, anger, pride, delusion and greed.
759.tie_back: The Kural calls wealth the sharpest steel for cutting down the pride of one's enemies; Jainism points the blade inward, telling one to cut down one's own pride and greed instead of external foes.
759.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
759._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; Jain teaching does not endorse using wealth against enemies, so this is an honest contrasting match that shares only the language of conquering foes and their pride.

760.quote_or_event: “Anyonya-pratibandhena trivargam sadhayan : Fulfilling the three-fold aim of life - that is, dharma, artha and kama - without excluding any of its elements.”
760.explanation: Hemacandra's ideal Jain householder pursues virtue, wealth and pleasure together in balance, none crowding out the others, alongside the first quality of honestly earned wealth.
760.tie_back: The Kural closes by saying that those with abundant honest wealth easily attain the other two aims of virtue and happiness, and the Jain householder code likewise holds the three aims together as one balanced pursuit.
760.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, no. 18, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)
760._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com (including the source's own hyphen spacing); a strong fit on the three aims of life, though the Jain item stresses balance rather than wealth making the other two easy, and for Jains the aims stay below the goal of liberation.
